questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the pH of the phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) used in haemagglutination assays is critical?

answers.a: pH affects the charge and integrity of sialic acid receptors on RBCs, influencing binding efficiency
answers.b: pH determines the concentration of red blood cells required
answers.c: pH controls the rate of complement activation
answers.d: pH affects only the colour of the RBC suspension and has no functional role

explanations.a: The pH of the PBS is critical because it directly influences the charge and structural integrity of the sialic acid receptors on RBC membranes.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to include a 'cell control' (RBCs only, no serum or virus) in a haemagglutination inhibition assay?

answers.a: To ensure RBCs do not spontaneously agglutinate and form a false-positive baseline
answers.b: To calculate the maximum possible HAU of the virus
answers.c: To serve as a positive control for inhibition
answers.d: To confirm that the diluent does not lyse RBCs

explanations.a: The cell control serves as a baseline check to verify that the RBCs do not spontaneously aggregate in the diluent, avoiding false positives.

questions.question: Which of the following viruses does NOT typically utilise sialic acid receptors and therefore cannot be detected by a conventional haemagglutination assay without modification?

explanations.d: Rabies virus does not bind to sialic acid receptors; it typically binds to acetylcholine receptors, so it cannot be detected by conventional HA.

questions.question: When reading a 96-well V-bottom plate HA assay, which result pattern indicates the endpoint (last well with complete agglutination)?

answers.a: A small, tight, red button at the very centre of the well
answers.b: A uniform red film coating the entire well floor with no streaming
answers.c: A partial ring of cells with streaming on tilting the plate
answers.d: A compact button forming only at the rim of the well

explanations.b: The endpoint of complete agglutination is shown by a uniform red film (mat) coating the well floor with no streaming when the plate is tilted.

questions.question: At what temperature is the haemagglutination assay for most influenza strains typically incubated to achieve optimal results?

explanations.b: Most influenza HA assays are incubated at room temperature (20–25°C) to allow optimal viral binding and lattice formation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of neuraminidase treatment of red blood cells before use in some haemagglutination assays?

answers.a: To increase RBC receptor density for influenza viruses
answers.b: To remove sialic acid receptors and prevent non-specific agglutination
answers.c: To fix RBCs and prolong shelf life
answers.d: To enhance complement receptor expression on the RBC surface

explanations.b: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues, helping to eliminate non-specific agglutination in certain serum assays.

questions.question: In a standard haemagglutination titration using 2-fold serial dilutions, if the HA titre is 1:64, how many one-unit (1 HAU) doses are present in the starting undiluted preparation?

explanations.c: A titer of 64 indicates that the undiluted sample can be diluted 64-fold to contain exactly 1 HAU (hemagglutinating unit). Thus, there are 64 HAU in the undiluted starting solution.

questions.question: What does a negative result appear as in a V-bottom microtiter plate?

answers.c: A compact button of cells at the center of the well
answers.d: Rim of cells along the edge

explanations.c: In the absence of agglutination, red blood cells settle under gravity to form a tight, compact red button at the center of a V-bottom well.

questions.question: Which microtiter plate is preferred for hemagglutination assays?

explanations.c: V-bottom or U-bottom wells are preferred because they allow non-agglutinated cells to settle clearly under gravity.

questions.question: What is the typical RBC concentration used in hemagglutination assays?

explanations.b: A concentration of 0.5% to 1.0% RBCs is typical for hemagglutination assays.
